young.html: Johan Huizinga (say HOW-zing-ah) was a Dutch historian. He loved old paintings and old chronicles, and he wanted to know: what did it feel like to be alive six hundred years ago?

He found a world of strong contrasts. Nights were truly dark, with no streetlights. Winter was bitter cold, and summer feasts were full of color. Great lords wore splendid clothes while beggars sat in the street. And all day long, church bells rang out the hours, calling people to prayer, to work, to celebrate, or to mourn.

young.html: A sound map. Sit quietly for five minutes, indoors or out, and list every sound you hear. Which of them tell you the time, or call people together? Then imagine your town six hundred years ago. What would you have heard instead?

full.html: Johan Huizinga (1872–1945) taught history at Groningen and Leiden. His masterpiece, published in Dutch in 1919, studies life, thought and art in France and the Low Countries, above all the court of the Dukes of Burgundy, in the 1300s and 1400s. F. Hopman's English version, The Waning of the Middle Ages (1924), was prepared with Huizinga's help and somewhat shortened; a full new translation appeared in 1996 as The Autumn of the Middle Ages. Huizinga later wrote Homo Ludens (1938), on play in culture. During the German occupation of the Netherlands he was held hostage, and he died in February 1945, a few months before the liberation.

full.text: To the world when it was half a thousand years younger, the outlines of all things seemed more clearly marked than to us. The contrast between suffering and joy, between adversity and happiness, appeared more striking.
full.author: Johan Huizinga
full.work: The Waning of the Middle Ages, Chapter I

full.html: Huizinga paints a world of extremes: dark and light, quiet and noise, cold and warmth, sickness and health, all felt more sharply than today. Life was public and full of ceremony; rank was shown in dress; feelings swung fast between tears and joy, cruelty and tenderness.

full.text: One sound rose ceaselessly above the noises of busy life and lifted all things unto a sphere of order and serenity: the sound of bells.

full.html: Many people of that time, Huizinga says, felt the world was growing worse. He sees three paths they took: turning away from the world toward God; trying to reform it; or dreaming it more beautiful, living as if life were an ideal story. The great example of the third path is chivalry, the ideal of the brave, loyal, courteous knight, which nobles acted out in tournaments, orders of knighthood and splendid vows, even as real warfare was changing.

Religious thought, Huizinga argues, had become crowded with images and symbols: every object could point to a sacred meaning. The age was also full of reminders of death, such as the painted "dance of death," in which people of every rank are led away together. He handles these with care, and so do we.

The usual story treated the 1400s in the North as the start of the Renaissance. Huizinga argues the reverse: the art of Jan van Eyck and the culture of the Burgundian court were the rich, overripe end of the Middle Ages, an autumn rather than a spring.

The book is admired as one of the great works of history writing, praised for bringing a whole period to life through its feelings, ceremonies and images. Historians have also criticized it: it draws mostly on court chronicles, poems and paintings made for the elite, so it says little about peasants and townspeople or about economic life; its picture of a "childlike" age of extreme emotions is now seen as overdrawn; and the idea of the period as a decline is disputed, since the same centuries saw growth in trade, cities and learning. It remains a classic and a model of cultural history.
Thinking Huizinga called the late Middle Ages a gloomy dark age. He loved its art and found it full of splendor; his "autumn" is a season of ripeness as well as ending.

items: Chaucer and Dante, on the Middle Ages rungs, show the ideals and images Huizinga studies from inside.
Gibbon's Decline and Fall, in the 18th-century rungs, also studied an age as an ending; compare their views of decline.
Burckhardt, the Swiss historian, had pictured the Italian Renaissance as the birth of the modern individual; Huizinga answered from the North.
The Art Ladder topics on books of hours, the Northern Renaissance and Gothic architecture show the art he wrote about.
Can a historian know how people of the past felt?
Is an age an "autumn" or a "spring" depending on where you stand?
Why do people dream of a better world in hard times?
What do the sounds and ceremonies of a place tell us about its people?

questions: What sounds tell you the time of day where you live?
Why might feelings have seemed sharper in a world with dark nights and cold winters?
What ideals, like chivalry, do people today try to live up to?
Huizinga used paintings and poems as evidence. What else would you want, to know how ordinary people lived?
Is the end of something always sad? Can it also be ripe and beautiful?
